title: SnO2-Modified Two-Dimensional CuO for Enhanced Electrochemical Reduction of CO2 to C2H4
abstract: Electrochemical reduction of CO2 was a widespread method for CO2 conversion into valuable chemical fuel. C2H4 is an important product from CO2 reduction. However, conversion of CO2 into the hydrocarbon C2H4 faced large energy barriers. Herein, we, for the first time, achieve a high efficiency for electrochemical conversion of CO2 to C2H4 on a tin-modified CuO. By modifying with Sn, we obtained a related low onset potential of C2H4 as positive as −0.8 V versus RHE and a high Faradaic efficiency of C2H4 as high as 22% at −1.0 V (vs RHE). According to density functional calculation, the Sn dopant mainly enriched the electron density of CuO, while it was electron-poor in the Sn dopants. The rate of CO2 reduction can be enhanced on Cu nanosheets with higher electron density. We believed that this work would promote the development of two-dimensional catalysts for CO2 conversion and deepen the understanding of doping on CO2 reduction.

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
The widespread use of fossil energy leads to more and more anthropogenic carbon emissions. This had caused serious global warming. It was more and more important to substitute traditional fossil fuel energy with renewable energy including wind, solar, and hydroelectricity gradually. However, their long-term storage remained a challenge because of the seasonal change of renewable energy sources.1,2 As a carbon capture technology, the carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR) offered a potential strategy.3 Electrochemical CO2RR was one of the most promising strategies to convert CO2 into energy such as CH4, C2H4, and so on. To obtain high activity in electrochemical CO2 reduction, the key point was to develop high-efficiency electrocatalysts because they could lower the energetic barriers for CO2 conversion. The electrochemical reduction process involved multisteps, and high-efficiency electrocatalysts could stabilize the intermediates and transition states.4 Therefore, efficient electrocatalysts were crucial because they were able to accelerate sluggish reaction kinetics and promote the product selectivity. Many catalysts including Au, Ag, Cu, Zn, Sn, and Co were active for CO2 electroreduction. 5−10 Usually, CO was the most common and easily accessible product because it did not involve a proton introduction process. To obtain hydrocarbons such as C2H4, we need to control the reaction pathways, reduce reaction overpotentials, and develop electrocatalysts with higher substrate selectivity. Cu was generally considered to be able to produce a significant amount of hydrocarbons.11 Recently, it has been reported that CuOx should be efficient electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction with hydrocarbon selectivity
at low temperature,12 but it still had some disadvantages such as high overpotential and low C2+ selectivity. Therefore, it was necessary to develop efficient catalysts with high activity, selectivity, and stability. Synthesis of nanomaterials was an effective method to achieve high activity and selectivity, such as nanowires13 and nanoparticles.14 Nanomaterial electrocatalysts exhibited good metallic conductivity and plenty of active sites15−18 but also enlarged the surface area and stability.19−21 For example, a two-dimensional material with a certain facet exposed has the potential to exhibit high selectivity toward CO2 reduction. Besides, doping was an effective method to manipulate the increase in efficiency and selectivity of CO2 reduction. Specifically for CuO, there were only some reports about nonmetal doping such as N and S.22,23 However, the function of the dopant on CO2 reduction was still not clear. Also, there were hardly any reports about metal-doped CuO for CO2 reduction. In this work, CuO nanosheets (NSs) with the (−400) facet
dominating was first prepared; then, it started to produce C2H4 at a small bias of −0.8 V (vs reversible hydrogen electrode, RHE). Its bulk counterpart hardly produced any C2H4 within a

These catalysts exhibited the best onset potential and Faradaic efficiency toward C2H4 generation among copper metal and copper oxide electrolysts.4,24−26 A very low onset potential of as positive as −0.8 V (vs RHE) was obtained for C2H4 production, and a Faradaic efficiency for C2H4 generation of about 24% was achieved at −1.0 V versus RHE. The mechanism for the enhancement and selectivity induced by Sn doping was systematically investigated, and an explanation was provided.

sections.heading: 2. MATERIALS AND METHODS
sections.text:
2.1. Synthesis of Sn−CuO NSs. All the reagents were commercially obtained and directly used, and no further purification was needed. SnO2-decorated CuO NSs were synthesized by a onestep hydrothermal method. CuCl2·2H2O (6 mmol) and a certain volume of 0.2 M SnO2·2H2O solution were mixed with each other and dissolved in 20 mL of deionized water. After magnetic stirring, the pH was adjusted to 13 using 0.4 M NaOH solution. Then, the solution was moved to a 50 mL Teflon-lined stainless steel autoclave and heated at 180 °C for 6 h. The products were collected via centrifugation and washed with deionized water and absolute ethanol several times. The product was then dried in vacuum at 80 °C overnight. 2.2. Characterization. The X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) patterns were recorded via a Rigaku Smartlab X-ray diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation. The field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) images were obtained using a ZEISS Gemini-300 scanning electron microscope. A JEM-2100 transmission electron microscope was used to obtain the transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images and high-resolution TEM images. An acceleration voltage of 200 kV was produced using a tungsten filament. X-ray photoelectron spectral (XPS) data were collected from ES-CALAB 250Xi (Thermo Fischer) with Al Kα (hυ = 1253.6 eV) as the excitation source. 2.3. Electrochemical Measurements. An Autolab potentiostat (PGSTAT-302N, EcoChemie) was used to carry out the electrochemical measurements. A three-electrode configuration and 0.5 M KHCO3 solution (pH ≈ 6.86) in a H-type cell were used. A Nafion 117 proton exchange membrane was used in the H-type cell for separation. The catalyst solution was prepared by dissolving pure water (200 μL), isopropyl alcohol (200 μL), catalyst (1 mg), and Nafion solution (5.5 μL, 5 wt %, Fuel Cell Earth) in a glass vial. After 10 min of sonication, the ink was painted on a gas diffusion layer (the geometric area was 1 cm2). A platinum plate was used as the counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl) was utilized as the reference electrode. The potentials measured against the reference electrode were converted into the RHE scale according to the Nernst equation (eq 1)17

2.4. Theoretical Calculations. The density function calculation was performed using a VASP package.34 The projector-augmented wave method with Perdew−Burke−Ernzerh of the GGA functional was used.35−37 Electronic convergence was 1 × 10−5 eV.38,39 The optimization of the crystal structure can be considered to be acceptable when the Hellmann−Feynman force achieves a value smaller than 1 × 10−2 eV Å−1. A CuO and Sn-doped CuO slab was constructed. The vacuum region was about 15 Å in height.

sections.heading: 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
3.1. Structure and Morphology. The SEM images of bulk CuO and CuO NSs are shown in Figure S1. Compared with bulk CuO (Figure S1a), CuO NSs exhibited apparent two-dimensional structures. This could be seen more clearly in the TEM image (Figure 1a). The microstructure of SnO2− CuO became much smaller than that of CuO. Energydispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) mapping demonstrated the presence of tin in the decorated sample with 3% Sn (Figure S2). This result confirmed the presence of copper, oxide, and tin in the catalyst. The TEM images confirmed the typical sheet structure of catalysis. The TEM images of CuO and SnO2−CuO NS catalysts are shown in Figures 1 and S3, respectively.

The theoretical value of the angle between (002) and (021) was calculated to be about 69.69°, while the measured angle in the TEM image was about 69.00°. The close values confirmed the two facets to be (002) and (021). Therefore, the plane of the CuO NS could be calculated to be (002) × (021) = (−400). Owing to its NS morphology, it could enlarge the surface area and enhance electrochemical activity.19,40
The XRD patterns are shown in Figures 2 and S4. For the CuO NS, there were nine reflection peaks corresponding to (002) and (111) directions.41−45 There was no obvious peak of SnO2 in the XRD pattern because of its low content in the samples.9 To explore the surface composition of catalysts, the XPS spectra were measured. The XPS analysis revealed intense Cu 2p peaks at 931.9 and 951.6 eV corresponding to Cu 2p3/2 and 2p1/2, respectively. The satellite peak at 942.8 eV was ascribed to the shake-up line of CuO.46 The peaks at 495.4 and 487.2 eV indicated the binding energies of Sn 3d5/2 and Sn 3d3/2, respectively, which correspond to Sn
4+.9,46,47 The O 1s spectra (Figure S5) were deconvoluted into two distinct peaks (3% SnO2−CuO NS). The first one at 529.7 ± 0.2 eV could be assigned to lattice oxygen in metal oxide, whereas the other one at 531.1 ± 0.3 eV should be O2− ions or/and hydroxyls.9,48
3.2. Activity for CO2 Reduction. Chronoamperometric electrolysis was performed using an H-type divided cell in 0.5 M KHCO3 CO2-saturated solution. The working electrode potential was in the range between −0.2 and −1.0 V (vs RHE) at an interval of 0.2 V (Figures 3 and S6). The current density for CO2 electroreduction became higher at more negative potential. Bulk CuO has the lowest current density, and it could only convert CO2 into CO with a low Faradaic
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsami.0c09240 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
C
efficiency. The Faradaic efficiency of CO generation was only as low as 4% at 0.8 V (vs RHE), and no C2H4 was detected within the applied potential window. CuO NSs display appreciable improvement over their bulk counterpart. CuO NSs are capable of producing hydrocarbon of C2H4 with a Faradaic efficiency of 2.7% at −0.8 V (vs RHE) and 4.5% at −1.0 V (vs RHE). Also, they exhibited a 12% Faradaic efficiency of CO (Figure 3c), which was three times higher than that of bulk CuO at −0.8 V (vs RHE). In addition, these results clearly indicated the advantage of the NS structure. Doping of Sn further increased the activity. The 3% SnO2− CuO NS exhibited an onset potential of as positive as −0.8 V (vs RHE) for C2H4. When the electrode potential was more negative at −1.0 V (vs RHE), Faradaic efficiency of C2H4 went to 22%.4,47,49,50 Besides C2H4, the 3% SnO2−CuO NS exhibited an onset potential for CO generation at −0.55 V (vs RHE) (Figure S7). In this work, Faradaic efficiency of the 3% SnO2−CuO NS for CO generation was 12% at −0.6 V (vs RHE). When the applied potential shifted to −0.8 V (vs RHE), Faradaic efficiency for CO generation was 28% and C2H4 was 8%. As the electrode potential went to −0.8 V (vs RHE), CO became the dominant CO2 reduction product. A volcano relationship was found between the Faradaic efficiencies of CO. At more negative potential, the main product was C2H4. With regard to the content of Sn, the optimum content of tin was 3% for both C2H4 and CO. The partial current density for C2H4 and CO formation with the 3% SnO2−CuO NS was higher than that obtained with other catalysts (Figure S8). Compared with other reports (Table S1), tin-decorated CuO NSs improve the activity and selectivity of CO2 electroreduction to C2H4 because of the synergetic effect between tin and copper. In the long-term experiment (Figure S9), the current density was stable, and their faradic efficiencies for producing CO and C2H4 were always higher than 20 and 10%, respectively (Figure S10). This indicated that the catalysts exhibited high stability in the long-time reaction. There were no changes in the peaks of Sn 3d, O 1s (Figure S5), and Cu 2p (Figure S11), which indicated the stability of the as-prepared catalysts. Hydrogen was a byproduct generated in CO2 reduction reaction in aqueous solution (Figure S12). When the potential was more negative, the Faradaic efficiency of products for CO2 reduction became higher and hydrogen evolution could be simultaneously suppressed by SnO2−CuO catalysis, especially the 3% SnO2−CuO NS (Figure 3d).16,48,51 The Faradaic efficiency of previously reported tin- and copper-based materials is summarized in Figure 4 (Table S1). As shown in Figure 4, the main products in the CO2 electroreduction process on tin and copper catalysts included CH4, alcohols, C2H4, CO, and HCOOH.
47,49,51−55 Concerning C2H4, our SnO2-doped CuO exhibited an onset potential at as early as −0.8 V (vs RHE).4,51,53 In this work, with the catalyst of the 3% SnO2−CuO NS, the onset potential of CO shifted positively to −0.55 V (vs RHE), and the Faradaic efficiency of CO was 12% at −0.6 V (vs RHE), which was lower than that in other reports.24,26,46,49,51 When the applied potential shifted at −0.8 V (vs RHE), Faradaic efficiency of CO was 28% and C2H4 was also detected. Faradaic efficiency of C2H4 went to 22% at −1.0 V (vs RHE), and the potential was more positive than that of other reports.29,42,51
3.3. CO2 Adsorption Ability. The enhancement mechanism was studied by recording the Tafel slopes and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV).
We find that the adsorption of CO2 was crucial for its electroreduction. As indicated in Figure 5a, Tafel slopes of the as-prepared samples were larger than 118 mV/dec. This indicated that the adsorbed intermediate CO2 induced by onelectron transfer should be the rate-determining step.56 The Tafel slope of CuO NSs (232 mV/dec) was smaller than their bulk counterpart, indicating the faster kinetics for NSs. Notably, the 3% SnO2−CuO NS and 5% SnO2−CuO NS displayed a much lower Tafel slope than other samples. This corresponded to a higher activity in CO2 electroreduction. Herein, SnO2−CuO samples showed a higher kinetic activity and significantly lower Tafel slope, indicating that the synergistic effect between Sn and Cu significantly promoted the kinetic activity for reduction reactions.44,47,57 The LSV was recorded in Ar-saturated and CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution. The large cathodic peaks (LSV in Figure S13) between −0.1 and −0.3 V (vs RHE) should be ascribed to the reduction of oxide species.50,58 Concerning Sn doping, the peak intensity was similar for Sn-free and SnO2-modified CuO. In the process of the CO2-saturated electrolyte (Figure 5b), the cathodic peak increased appreciably, which should be attributed to CO2 adsorption. The increase was more obvious for the SnO2-modified sample, especially the CuO with 3 and 1% Sn modified. The onset potential shifted to more positive with increasing the amount of tin (Figure 5b). This strongly suggested that doping of tin should be beneficial to CO2 adsorption.35 Compared with the process of Ar, the current density and onset potential of 3% SnO2−CuO were higher in the presence of CO2-saturated solution than that in Ar. The ability of different samples to adsorb CO2 was further evaluated by plotting the LSV curves after ECSA correction (Figure 5c). By measuring the double-layer capacitance, the ECSA could be evaluated.32,33 The LSV curves after ECSA correction illustrated the highest intrinsic catalytic activity of the 3% SnO2−CuO NS among these samples, implying that the ability of Sn-doped CuO was superior to Sn-free CuO in CO2 adsorption.
3.4. Mechanism for the Enhancement of SnO2−CuO. We propose that the Sn-inducing promotion of CO2 reduction should be ascribed to three reasons:
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsami.0c09240 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
D
First, doping of SnO2 leads to smaller CuO and greatly lowers the resistance of charge transfer in CuO. The EIS spectra of catalysis were obtained (Figure 5d). The curves included semi-arc and linear sections in high- and lowfrequency regions, respectively. In the EIS spectra of the 3% SnO2−CuO NS, a small real axis intercept and small radius of the semicircle indicated small internal resistance of solution and faster charge transfer. Also, the larger slope in the linear part indicated rapid mass diffusion.26 The impedance values of other samples were all higher than that of the 3% SnO2−CuO NS. Therefore, an appropriate decoration ratio of tin could enlarge the contact area and shorten the charge transfer distance. Second, Sn optimized the charge distribution in Cu and subsequently promoted CO2 activation. The detailed study was investigated by density functional calculation. As discussed above, CO2 molecules were required to be adsorbed on the surface for further reduction. In our calculation, after optimization, the average length of the C−O bond in the CO2 molecules (0.163) was elongated to 0.1181 nm on the surface of CuO and to 0.1183 nm on the SnO2-modified CuO substrate (Figure 6). The elongation of the C−O bond demonstrated the activation of the CO2 molecules on the surface of catalysts.59
3.5. Explanation for the Selectivity of Sn−CuO. The selectivity of Sn-doped CuO was further investigated by density functional calculation. Previous reports pointed out that HCOOH was preferentially produced on Sn-based materials. However, we did not detect any HCOOH in our work. In contrast, our sample exhibited excellent activity in producing C2H4 and CO. As gas products, they could be easily separated. Besides, using mature chemical technologies, they could be further transferred into fuels and bulk chemicals at a large scale.51
The reason for the selectivity by doping with Sn was investigated by analyzing the charge distribution. We discovered that the doping of Sn causes a redistribution of charge in the CuO. In the charge density map (Figure S14), the charge represented by the yellow region distributes
uniformly in the CuO substrate. In contrast, the charge mainly concentrated on O and Cu atoms, while it was bare on the Sn atoms. It was indicated that electrons are donated from Sn to other atoms. This could also be reflected in the Bader charge analysis. As shown in Table 1, in CuO, the state of Cu decreased, reflecting the loss of electrons in Cu atoms, while that of O increases, reflecting the gain of electrons. This result suggested the migration of electrons from Cu to O. This was in consistence with the ionic bond of Cu−O. With respect to Sndoped CuO, the average value of state for Sn was as small as
0.08, which confirmed the loss of electrons and was in good agreement with the charge density map. The state for O increased from 7.02 to 7.09 and that for Cu increased from 9.97 to 9.99 when compared with Sn-free CuO. Therefore, the abovementioned discussion demonstrated that the doping of Sn results in the gain of electrons on the Cu and O atoms. Generally, CO2 molecules were preferentially activated in the electron-rich region. Consequently, when a CO2 molecule was close to the SnO2-modified CuO substrate, we observed an appreciable yellow region between the CO2 molecule and a Cu atom near the Sn in the charge difference map, suggesting that CO2 is activated on the site. The doping of Sn caused the increase in charge density in Cu in its vicinity, which was beneficial to CO2 reduction. It was well known that CO2 molecules should be reduced by accepting electrons from the surface of catalysts. For the Sndoped CuO, the function of Sn was to increase the electron density in CuO. Therefore, it was reasonable that CO2 still tends to occur on CuO. According to previous reports, Sn tended to produce HCOOH, while Cu tended to produce C2H4. Hence, it should be the reason why doping of Sn tends to increase the Faradaic efficiency of CO and C2H4 but not HCOOH. In the partial density of states (PDOS), the DOS of Cu
atoms and the CO2 atoms (including C and O) overlap each other, confirming the formation of bonding between them (Figures 7 and S15).60 When a CO2 molecule was adsorbed on the surface, the electronic state of CO2 would interact with the atoms from the substrate. Then, the hybridized energy levels split into antibonding states (σ*) located above the Fermi level and bonding states (σ) located below the Fermi level. According to literature studies,50,51,54 the closer the highest peak of bonding states for the CO2, the stronger interaction between the substrate and the adsorbed molecules.61 The peak of DOS for O was located at −6.95 eV for Sn-free and −6.87 eV for Sn-containing samples. The smaller value for the SnO2modified CuO sample indicated a stronger bonding between
CO2 and the substrate. 62 It confirmed that the doping of Sn should be favorable for CO2 activation. The bonding energy of molecules adsorbed on SnO2−CuO is calculated according to the following formula, eq 4
= − −E E E Etot substrate molecule (4) where Ead is the binding energy, Etot is the overall energy of the molecule on the Sn−CuO substrate, Esubstrate corresponds to the energy of the substrate, and Emolecule is the energy of the intermediates adsorbed. The reduction of CO2 to CO was a simple one-step process. The Ead of CO2 was found to be −0.12 eV. The Ead of CO was −0.27 eV. The downhill of energy suggested that the reduction of CO2 to CO should be favorable. The reduction of CO2 to C2H4 was a multistep process involving several intermediates. Because of our calculation resource limitation, we only chose some key steps to study. The linking of two carbon atoms leads to the intermediate CO−CHO (Figure S16). It would transfer to C−C.63 These two intermediates were reported to be the key steps for the formation of C2H4. The binding energy of CO−CHO was about −0.62 eV, and the binding energy dropped to −1.28 eV for the C−C intermediate. They were much lower than CO. This indicated that the formation of the C−C intermediate should be thermodynamically favorable. The binding energy of C2H4 was about −0.37 eV. Compared with the C−C intermediate, the free energy needed to go uphill. However, the energy for C2H4 (−0.37 eV) was lower than the binding energy for CO (−0.27 eV), suggesting that the generation of C2H4 was easier.

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
In summary, a simple and potentially synthetic method had been developed for tin-decorated CuO NSs. CuO decorated with a proper content of tin exhibited remarkably higher selectivity and activity compared to CuO catalysts. Further studies investigated that the synergetic effect between SnO2 and CuO should be beneficial to CO2 electroreduction. The
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsami.0c09240 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
F
high activity from NSs enhanced CO2 •− adsorption. The tuning of the ratio of the tin-modified CuO NS would be further exploited for the development of selective CO2 reduction electrocatalysts.
